cases.title: Karimenu II dam: land taken in Gatundu North and compensation still unpaid
cases.place: Gituamba ward, Gatundu North, Kiambu County, Kenya
cases.point: The Karimenu II Dam reservoir in Gituamba ward, Gatundu North (OpenStreetMap way 1423111416, through Nominatim). The Star names Kiriko, Gathanji, Buchana and Kariminu as the villages the dam is built in. AidData's coordinate for record 58737 is a village of the same name, Kiriko, about 66 km to the north-east in Kirinyaga County (OpenStreetMap node 44931883).

lenders.name: China Eximbank
lenders.role: AidData record 58737. A US$200,530,600 loan signed on 14 February 2017 to the AVIC & SMEDI joint venture, financing 85 per cent of a US$235,918,461 engineering, procurement, construction and financing contract; final maturity 21 July 2042, repayable in 20 equal half-yearly instalments. Disbursements of US$13,364,912 in Kenya's 2020-21 financial year and US$133,093,268 in 2021-22; US$158,254,011 outstanding at 30 June 2022. This is not a World Bank project and has no P-number.

cases.conditions: The loan went to the Chinese contractor rather than to the state: China Eximbank lent to the AVIC & SMEDI joint venture to cover 85 per cent of its own contract, with what AidData records as an apparent repayment guarantee from the Government of Kenya. An advance payment of 20 per cent of the contract, US$47,183,692, was made to the joint venture in mid-2017 against a bank guarantee. A Kenyan parliamentary committee inspected the site on 28 March 2019 and found no works had begun 24 months after the agreements were signed, and that the implementing agency had not issued a commencement letter to the contractor because of land acquisition difficulties; the committee asked the Auditor General for a special audit of the advance payments made before the land was acquired (AidData record 58737).

companies.name: AVIC International Holding Corporation
companies.role: Lead of the joint venture that held the engineering, procurement, construction and financing contract, which AidData records as signed on 24 April 2017 (AidData record 58737)

companies.name: Shanghai Municipal Engineering Design Institute (Group) Co., Ltd
companies.role: Joint venture partner on the same contract, responsible for design (AidData record 58737)

companies.name: Athi Water Works Development Agency
companies.role: Kenyan state water agency under the Ministry of Water and Sanitation that signed the contract and implemented the works; AidData's record names it in its earlier form, Athi Water Services Board

cases.community: The works needed 600 acres: 171 acres in the first phase for the dam embankment and water draw-off structures, and 429 acres in the second phase for the reservoir area (AidData record 58737). On 1 August 2019 the water cabinet secretary Simon Chelugui said 246 affected people had been paid Sh1.28 billion for 171.6 acres in phase one, and that valuation of phase two had only just been finished; residents said they would block the project until phase two was paid. Jackson Mbugua said phase one compensation had started in 2017 and was only finalised in 2019, and that they feared phase two would be paid after the dam was built. Zipporah Wanjiru said: "If they want us to allow them to continue, let them pay us our money. We are not against the project". Chelugui said the ministry had a budget for phase two and that the money would go to the National Land Commission once the valuation was done, and that the government "will not touch anyone's land or properties including the crops and trees grown on the land until they are fully compensated" (The Star, 1 August 2019). On 26 February 2020 the implementing agency said 228 of the 246 phase one claimants had been paid Sh1.09 billion and 28 were still unpaid - 18 of the original claimants and 10 more who arose from subdivided plots - so the contractor had access to 136.5 of the 171 acres, and that the 34.5 acres left out were the ones needed for the diversion tunnel, intake tower and bridge. The agency attributed the hold-up to the slow pace of land acquisition by the National Land Commission, to a lack of funds to compensate the 28, and to succession and family disputes (The Star, 26 February 2020). On 20 September 2023 Kiambu senator Karungo Thang'wa said 150 acres at Kianjuku in Gatundu North were affected by constant backflow from the finished dam, and that residents were suffering instead of benefiting; Gatanga MP Edward Muriu said the deadlock was a budgetary matter and that the compensation money would not be diverted, and Thang'wa said the meeting with the water principal secretary had agreed that the government would compensate those affected (The Star, 20 September 2023). On 13 September 2025 the agency's chief executive Joseph Kamau said people in the buffer zone, about 50 metres from the top water line, had still not been paid: "We have compensated where the water sits, but we have not compensated an area we usually call the buffer zone." He said the valuation had gone to the National Land Commission and he expected movement by October, and conceded the process was behind schedule. Simon Nguyai Timothy, one of those waiting, said he had come hoping the water minister would address the compensation and was disappointed. In September 2023 President William Ruto had directed the then water minister Alice Wahome to settle Sh4.2 billion owed to affected families (Capital FM, 13 September 2025).
cases.outcome: The dam was completed and commissioned in August 2022 (Capital FM, 13 September 2025). Compensation for the buffer zone around the reservoir was still unpaid in September 2025, with the valuation lodged with the National Land Commission (Capital FM).

cases.confidence_note: Two Kenyan news organisations and the implementing agency's own statements carry the unpaid compensation, so the harm does not rest on the lender's account. Two phase-one payment figures differ and both are given here: the water cabinet secretary said Sh1.28 billion to 246 people on 1 August 2019, and the agency said Sh1.09 billion to 228 people on 26 February 2020. Two dates are given for the construction contract: AidData records 24 April 2017 and The Star of 26 February 2020 says May 2017. AidData's record is the only source here for the second-phase figure, saying 429 acres were needed for the reservoir area and that residents who had surrendered 383 acres for phase two had still not been paid in early 2021; the record does not explain the difference between the two acreages. AidData also notes that two other databases give different face values for the same loan - SAIS-CARI US$31 million and Boston University US$229 million - and that it follows the US$200,530,600 recorded in Kenya's external public debt register.
cx: Karimenu II dam land acquisition and compensation
cases.ecosystem: The dam is 59 metres high and holds 26.5 million cubic metres on the Karimenu river, below its meeting with the Gathanje, Kagundu and Githanga streams (AidData record 58737). The senator for Kiambu reported 150 acres at Kianjuku affected by backflow from the reservoir (The Star, 20 September 2023).
cases.whole: The dam supplies 70 million litres of water a day to Gatundu, Juja, Ruiru and parts of Nairobi, which Capital FM reports as serving nearly one million people; AidData's record puts it at an additional 850,000 people. In February 2020 more than 500 local residents had jobs at the site as casual workers, machine operators, drivers and technicians; casuals earning Sh498 a day asked for Sh700, and earthmover operators earning Sh1,000 asked for Sh2,000, one driver saying they were still being paid at 2013 rates (The Star, 26 February 2020).

lenders_add.name: China Eximbank
lenders_add.role: AidData records 45520 and 95928. Two buyer's credit loans signed with the Government of Sri Lanka on 17 February 2011 for Section IV of the expressway, Pinnaduwa to Godagama: US$74,329,906 under agreement BLA201011 for Package 1, Pinnaduwa to Kodagoda (km 30.8 to 45), and US$55,369,520 under agreement BLA201012 for Package 2, Kodagoda to Godagama (km 45 to 61.05) plus the balance of work on the Galle port access road. Both carried six-month LIBOR plus a 2.40 per cent margin, a 15-year maturity, a four-year grace period, a 0.7 per cent commitment fee, a 0.3 per cent management fee and a 6 per cent Sinosure premium. Sri Lanka's pre-emptive default announced on 12 April 2022 reportedly affected all China Eximbank loans with amounts outstanding at the time.

fields_add.conditions: China Eximbank financed Section IV of the expressway, from Pinnaduwa to Godagama, under two buyer's credit loans signed in February 2011. China National Technical Import & Export Corporation held the engineering, procurement and construction contract for both packages, signed on 11 June 2010, started work in April 2011 and finished in January 2014; that section opened to traffic on 16 March 2014 (AidData records 45520 and 95928).
fields_add.confidence_note: The displacement findings here are the Compliance Review Panel's, on the Asian Development Bank's loan, and the Panel reported in 2005. China Eximbank's two loans were signed in February 2011 and financed Section IV of the expressway, from Pinnaduwa to Godagama, which opened to traffic in March 2014. AidData's records for those two loans record no land acquisition or resettlement on that section.

lenders_add.name: China National Petroleum Corporation
lenders_add.role: AidData record 34197. This Chinese state-owned company pledged US$32 million in 2013 to compensate farmers whose land was taken for the pipelines and the railway works built for them. AidData records it as a grant with a commitment date of 1 January 2013, carries it at the status "Pipeline: Pledge", and says whether the pledged sum was delivered is unclear.

sources_add.title: Farmers Demand Compensation for Farmland Destroyed by Gas Pipeline

fields_add.community: China National Petroleum Corporation pledged US$32 million in 2013 to compensate farmers displaced by the works. AidData's record says local officials reported residents were paid in full at 4 million kyat, about US$4,625, for each hectare of land lost, that some residents said they received nothing, and that a CNPC official said compensating former landowners was difficult because most land on Maday Island was registered as vacant and most residents had no ownership documents; AidData is the only source here carrying those figures and says it is unclear whether the pledge was paid. About 400 people protested on 18 April 2013, saying they were inadequately compensated for their land and that they had been paid for only half of the 400 acres expropriated for the project, including a mountain owned by Maday Island residents, which CNPC representatives denied, saying the company had paid in full; they also asked for better transport from the Maday Island crude oil jetty to the villages of Kyauttan, Ywarma and Panhteinse, for electricity, and for more local jobs at better pay. On 2 August 2013 representatives of 30 villages delivered a list of demands to township, district and party offices in Kyaukpyu, asking for schools, clinics, roads between the villages, drinking water and electricity as compensation for the pipeline; Maung Aye of their Local Development Committee said they asked for an answer within 15 days, and officials of Myanma Oil and Gas Enterprise and of Daewoo International refused to accept the letter, saying it was a matter for local authorities (Radio Free Asia, 2 August 2013). On 19 February 2015 fifty farmers from 12 villages in Kyaukpyu township demonstrated outside the township administration office over farmland buried in mud by the pipeline construction and not paid for. One, U San Shwe, said they had claimed three times already. Farmers whose land was covered in mud had been paid in September 2013 and a Chinese gas company had paid 385,000 kyat an acre of mud-covered paddy, but nothing had been paid for that season's crop. U Wai Dawn of Pyar-Tae village said: "We are being squeezed between the company and the government". The deputy township administrator told the farmers that a complaint letter listing the damaged farmland had been sent from township to district level and was being examined, and the head of the township agriculture department told them the compensation was being processed and they would get it; the report adds that Myanma Oil and Gas Enterprise had paid for mud-covered farmland in 2012 and 2013 (Narinjara, 24 February 2015).
fields_add.suppression: On 19 April 2013 authorities in Kyaukpyu charged six villagers, said to be organisers of the protest held the day before, with illegal assembly for marching without a permit; the villagers had applied for permits in December at township and state level and were refused both times, and a number of Maday Island residents who worked as labourers for CNPC were reportedly dismissed after the protest (Radio Free Asia, 2 August 2013). Radio Free Asia reported on 26 September 2013 that a court in Kyaukpyu township had jailed ten people for three months each under Article 18 of the Peaceful Assembly Law over the same march. About 300 people from 20 villages gathered at the court demanding their release; one, Ko Nyi Nge, said that if the ten were not freed the authorities should arrest all the villagers who had protested. About 100 security force members and several firefighters ringed the court but did not act. Their lawyer Htein Lin said no witness testified that the ten had led the protest and said he would appeal. Human Rights Watch's deputy Asia director Phil Robertson said: "By jailing peaceful protesters, the Burmese government is creating a new class of political prisoners."
fields_add.confidence_note: The arrests, the jail sentences and the dismissal of CNPC labourers after the April 2013 protest are reported by Radio Free Asia, and the February 2015 protest over mud-damaged farmland by Narinjara. The two Radio Free Asia reports give six villagers charged in April 2013 and ten convicted in September 2013 over the same march. The US$32 million pledge and the 4 million kyat a hectare rate are carried only by AidData's record, which says it is unclear whether the pledge was delivered.
